# Root-contact subdivisions: exact geometry and two obstructions

This note concerns positive full-dimensional continuous fibers
`K_z subset R^d`, `d>=1`, at the finite positive index set `P`, after
replacing the original body by the convex hull of those fibers. Write
`r_z=|K_z|^(1/d)` and `Q=conv(P)`. No intrinsic extension is implicit.

## 1. The finite concave roof is well defined

Every integer point of `Q` belongs to `P`: any convex combination of
positive full-dimensional source fibers gives a positive body in the
target integer fiber. Thus `P=Q intersect Z^n`.

Define

    R(x)=max {sum_z lambda_z r_z:
               lambda_z>=0, sum lambda_z=1, sum lambda_z z=x}.

The feasible set is a nonempty compact simplex slice, so this maximum
is attained. The function is concave and piecewise affine, being the
upper roof of the convex hull of the finitely many lifted points
`(z,r_z)`. At every integer index `w in P`, Brunn--Minkowski and fiber
compatibility give

    sum_z lambda_z r_z<=r_w

for every feasible representation of `w`. The singleton representation
gives the reverse inequality, so `R(w)=r_w`.

Every maximal affine patch of this roof has an affine majorant `ell`
on the relative base space. If `E={z:r_z=ell(z)}`, the patch is exactly
`conv(E)`. One inclusion follows by taking convex combinations of the
contact points. For the other, an optimizing representation of any
point where `R=ell` can have positive weight only on contact indices,
since every gap `ell(z)-r_z` is nonnegative. These patches form the
usual finite polyhedral subdivision and cover `Q`.

The proved affine-root-majorant theorem applies on each patch: the
convex hull of the actual fiber centroids over `E` has singleton
sections at every integer base in `conv(E)`. The adjective “integer”
is essential. It cannot in general be removed.

## 2. One contact cell need not have an affine centroid section

Take `n=2,d=1`, `P={0,1}^2`, and give its four fibers length one with
centroid heights

    h_(0,0)=h_(1,1)=1,
    h_(1,0)=h_(0,1)=-1.

Let `C` be the convex hull of these four vertical intervals. Its base
projection is the unit square, whose only integer points are its four
vertices. Each vertex section is the prescribed interval. The body is
full dimensional in `R^3`: the four graph-centroid points already form
a tetrahedron with nonzero determinant, and vertical intervals can
only enlarge it.

Every integer root is one. Consequently the maximal root-contact cell
for the global majorant `ell=1` is the entire square. An affine scalar
function on a square has equal sums on its two diagonals, whereas these
centroid heights have diagonal sums `2` and `-2`. Hence no affine
section on this contact cell can take the four actual centroid values.

At the real base `(1/2,1/2)`, the convex hull of the centroids has the
whole interval of heights `[-1,1]`. The actual fiber is
`[-3/2,3/2]`: the two diagonal Minkowski averages provide the intervals
`[1/2,3/2]` and `[-3/2,-1/2]`, and all source heights lie in the stated
outer range. Thus its length is three, strictly larger than the roof
value one. This displays exactly why equality of the discrete roof at
integer bases cannot supply Brunn--Minkowski equality at real averages.

There is a compatible piecewise-affine centroid section after choosing
a triangulation using the integer graph vertices: affine interpolation
on each simplex lies in `C` by convexity. That general fact does not
make the original contact cell affine and does not make the full graph
lattice-convex across different simplices.

For comparison, a patch containing an integer point in its relative
interior does force an affine centroid section. To see this, let `G`
be the convex centroid hull and let its integer interior-base section
be a singleton. If another real-base section contained two points,
take a small positive convex weight on that base and a complementary
base in the patch so that their average is the interior integer point.
Combining either of the two graph points with one point over the
complementary base would give two points over the interior integer
base, a contradiction. Hence all sections are singletons, and convexity
of `G` then makes its section map affine. The unit-square example is
hollow and does not satisfy this extra hypothesis.

## 3. No constant fraction of mass need belong to one contact patch

For any integer `N>=1`, use one integer and one continuous coordinate,
indices `-N,...,N`, and symmetric intervals of lengths

    w_i=R-i^2,   R=(N+1)^2.

The piecewise-linear interpolation of this positive concave sequence
is concave. Its centered interval body is a full-dimensional convex
polygon whose actual integer fibers are exactly these intervals.
All centroid heights are zero; the actual mixed centroid also has
integer base zero by reflection symmetry.

Since `d=1`, the roots are the widths themselves. Their second
differences are strictly negative, so the roof has exactly `2N`
maximal affine cells, the consecutive unit intervals. An affine global
majorant can contact at most two sampled indices, and if it contacts
two then they must be adjacent: contact at nonadjacent indices would
force the intervening strictly concave sample strictly above the
affine majorant.

The largest possible contact mass is at most `2R`, while the total is
exactly

    M=(2N+1)R-N(N+1)(2N+1)/3
      =(2N+1)(N+1)(2N+3)/3.

Therefore every single contact patch has relative mass at most

    2R/M=6(N+1)/[(2N+1)(2N+3)] -> 0.

Already for fixed `n=1`, the number of maximal contact cells is
unbounded. Selecting one root-majorant contact graph and applying its
weighted Doignon estimate cannot retain a fixed positive fraction of
the total mass in this family. This says nothing against a new argument
that combines different patches with an additional proved invariant.

All fibers in these examples have positive full dimension. There is no
boundary-mass deletion or affine transformation of the integer lattice.
The examples obstruct the two specified intermediate mechanisms, not
OC.
